title: Billionaires Are Getting Medals. What’s Our Prize?
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott of Work Forward argues that overreach on AI is costing companies more than it returns and that the resulting backlash puts real gains for workers at risk. He starts with cost, noting that few firms can forecast their AI bills and that earning a market return on the build-out would require large output gains or labor cuts. He then shows that cost-cutting as a route to breakeven is self-defeating, citing survey data in which most HR leaders who cut jobs for AI would reconsider and many rehired the people they let go. Accounting rules that expense training but capitalize technology, he says, tilt executives toward investing in bots over people. Public opinion is souring, and he views the staged White House medal ceremony for tech titans as a symptom of leaders performing for power instead of workers. He closes with early findings that AI can help people thrive at work when leadership and culture are right, and that winning firms use AI to grow what each employee can deliver.
points: Cutting staff to cover AI costs is a prisoner's dilemma that damages employment, wages and the economy without actually paying the bill.
Survey evidence on AI-driven layoffs shows regret, lost skills and rehiring, which undercuts the productivity story and teaches remaining staff that AI is done to them.
Accounting rules that capitalize technology but expense training push executives to underinvest in developing people.
Whether AI helps or harms people at work depends on leadership and culture, not on the technology alone.
Firms that succeed with AI mostly use it to expand what each employee can deliver and to grow, rather than to streamline and cut.
quotes: If there’s one thing the executives I talk with agree on about AI, it’s that almost no one has a handle on the bill, let alone the ROI.

If we try to reach “breakeven” on AI through cost-cutting, employment and wages plummet, the economy takes a nose-dive, and the bill never actually gets covered (not to mention the massive unrest). In this Prisoner’s Dilemma, we all go to prison.

Accounting and tax rules are partly to blame. We capitalize and depreciate investments in technology but expense training, so building software doesn’t hit short-term results the way developing people does.
About 75% had made cuts tied to AI, yet “9 in 10 would rethink cuts related to AI if they were given the chance,” and 32% said they’d lost critical skills.
Every round of cuts like this also teaches the people who stay that AI is something done to them rather than for them, and resistance grows.

Leaders are growing revenue and headcount faster than their peers, with far better shareholder returns. Your focus on efficiency is my opening to take your customers with better products and services.

None of that makes AI bad for people at work. The danger is that the backlash throws out the real gains along with the hype, right when we could, god forbid, invest as much in the humans as we do in the bots.
AI on its own doesn’t harm people at work; like any technology, leadership and culture determine whether it makes people’s work (and lives) better or worse.
